explanation_text: The Miao silver horn headdress is built from rings stacked in layers, and each layer sits in a place that shapes the whole crown. Just as each digit's place gives a number its value, each ring has a position that shapes the headdress.
image_prompt: Illustrate a Miao silver horn headdress with ring layers labeled as ones, tens, and hundreds, showing how position affects value.

miao_culture: Adding silver rings to a bracelet
explanation_text: When a Miao girl adds silver rings to her bracelet, the total number grows; when she removes some, it shrinks. This is exactly how addition increases a total and subtraction decreases it.
image_prompt: Show a Miao bracelet gaining and losing silver rings, with the total number changing accordingly.

explanation_text: Laying out identical rows of Miao embroidery stitches shows multiplication as repeated groups. Splitting the stitches evenly among different pattern sections shows division.
image_prompt: Display rows of identical embroidered stitches arranged evenly, showing equal grouping (multiplication) and even sharing (division).

explanation_text: Miao women often wear silver bracelets in pairs, one on each arm. Bracelets lined up in pairs represent even numbers; a single leftover bracelet represents an odd number.
image_prompt: Show silver bracelets standing in pairs, with one single bracelet at the end to represent an odd number.

explanation_text: The geometric motifs that repeat around a batik cloth border follow rhythmic sequences. Counting every 5th motif is a natural way to see skip counting in action.
image_prompt: Show a batik border with repeating geometric motifs, highlighting every 5th pattern to illustrate skip counting.

miao_culture: Silver neck rings of different sizes
explanation_text: The silver neck rings a Miao woman wears are stacked from smallest to largest. Comparing the sizes of the rings shows which is greater or smaller, just like comparing numbers.
image_prompt: Show several silver neck rings of different sizes, using > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: When a batik artist estimates how much wax and indigo dye to prepare for a piece of cloth, she rounds to a convenient amount. This mirrors rounding a number to a nearby, easier value.
image_prompt: Show a batik artist preparing indigo dye, roughly estimating the amount and labeling it with rounded amounts.

explanation_text: When silver ornaments are shared equally among sisters, each person receives a fraction of the total collection. Each share is one part of the whole.
image_prompt: Show a collection of silver ornaments divided into equal shares among several girls, each labeled as a fraction of the whole.

explanation_text: Dividing a piece of cloth for embroidery into 2 equal parts or into 4 smaller equal parts gives the same total amount. These are equivalent fractions.
image_prompt: Show a cloth panel divided first into halves, then into quarters, demonstrating equal portions.

explanation_text: If small bundles of thread are gathered into larger bundles, you simplify the count of bundles. This is like reducing a fraction to its simplest form.
image_prompt: Depict smaller bundles of thread merging into one larger bundle, labeled with reduced fractions.

miao_culture: Full and half baskets of rice
explanation_text: If a harvest fills 3 full baskets of rice and half a basket more, that is 3½. A whole number together with a fraction is a mixed number.
image_prompt: Show three full rice baskets and one half-full basket labeled as 3½.

explanation_text: When harvested rice fills more than one basket but is counted in equal basket-sized parts, the total is greater than one whole. This is an improper fraction.
image_prompt: Show several small baskets filled past one full portion, symbolizing fractions greater than 1.

explanation_text: Adding portions of dyed yarn from different bundles shows how fractional amounts combine into a larger amount, and eventually into a whole.
image_prompt: Show smaller bundles of dyed yarn being combined to make one total bundle.

miao_culture: Using part of a dye cake
explanation_text: When a batik artist uses part of an indigo dye cake, the remaining portion is the difference. Removing a part from a whole shows fraction subtraction.
image_prompt: Show an indigo dye cake with a portion cut away, the remainder labeled as the fraction left.

miao_culture: Half of a half portion of cloth
explanation_text: If each piece of cloth is half of half a bolt of fabric, you are finding a fraction of a fraction. Multiplying fractions finds a part of a part.
image_prompt: Show a bolt of cloth divided into halves, and one half divided again to show smaller portions.

explanation_text: If one rice cake is cut evenly into smaller pieces, you are dividing a fraction by another fraction. Each cut asks how many smaller pieces fit into the whole.
image_prompt: Show rice cakes being cut into smaller even pieces to illustrate fractional division.

explanation_text: Measuring indigo dye and water in liters and milliliters introduces decimals. One and a half liters is written 1.5 liters.
image_prompt: Show a measuring container marked with 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 liters of dye.

explanation_text: Whether you say half a basket of rice or 0.5 baskets, both describe the same amount. Fractions and decimals are just two ways to write the same value.
image_prompt: Show two labeled baskets, one marked ½ and another 0.5, holding the same amount of rice.

explanation_text: When a student scores 90 out of 100 on a Miao language class test, that is 90%. Percents express parts per hundred.
image_prompt: Show a test paper with 90/100 written and a 90% mark beside it.

explanation_text: A 10% discount on a silver ornament at the Xijiang market shows how percents are used to find a part of a whole price.
image_prompt: Show a market stall sign with a silver ornament marked 10% off and price tags with reduced amounts.

explanation_text: If some baskets of grain are unlabeled, each one holds an unknown amount. A symbol that stands for an unknown quantity is a variable.
image_prompt: Show labeled grain baskets (2 and 3) and an unlabeled basket marked as x.

explanation_text: If you have 2 known baskets of grain and x more unknown ones, the total can be written as the expression 2 + x.
image_prompt: Show two grain baskets plus an unlabeled one, symbolized as 2 + x.

explanation_text: When two baskets hang in balance on a carrying pole, the weights are equal. Both sides of an equation represent the same balance.
image_prompt: Show a carrying pole with equal baskets on both sides labeled as an equation.

explanation_text: If one basket on a shoulder pole is heavier, you add or remove weight on that side to balance it. One adjustment solves a one-step equation.
image_prompt: Show a shoulder pole with uneven baskets being balanced by adding or removing one load.

explanation_text: Preparing a rice dish takes two steps: washing the rice first and then steaming it. Solving a two-step equation works the same way, one operation at a time.
image_prompt: Show the step sequence: wash rice then steam it then get the result, symbolizing step-by-step solving.

explanation_text: When one family's silver collection is larger than another's, the amounts are not equal. Comparing unequal amounts is exactly what inequalities describe.
image_prompt: Show two collections of silver ornaments of different sizes with > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: In batik you must draw the wax pattern before dyeing the cloth; the steps cannot be swapped. The order of operations follows the same idea of doing things in sequence.
image_prompt: Show a batik sequence where steps must happen in order, labeled like parentheses, exponents, etc.

explanation_text: If a missing silver button is replaced with an identical one, the outfit is unchanged. Replacing a letter with its number value is substitution.
image_prompt: Show a missing silver button replaced with an identical one, representing substitution.

explanation_text: Each silver dot pressed into a Miao headdress marks a fixed position, just like a point marks an exact location in geometry.
image_prompt: Show a silver headdress with individual dots labeled as points on a coordinate grid.

explanation_text: Warp threads stretched straight across a weaving loom run in both directions. These taut threads resemble geometric lines that extend without end.
image_prompt: Show straight warp threads stretched on a loom, representing geometric lines.

explanation_text: When the wooden door of a Miao stilt house opens, it forms an angle between the door and the door frame.
image_prompt: Show a wooden stilt-house door partially open with the angle clearly marked.

explanation_text: The wooden beams meeting at right angles in a Miao house frame form perpendicular lines, giving the structure its strength.
image_prompt: Show house frame beams meeting at 90° angles.

explanation_text: The stone edges of terraced rice fields in the mountains run side by side and never meet. They are parallel lines.
image_prompt: Show parallel stone terraces of rice fields running side by side down a mountainside.

explanation_text: Seen from above, the courtyards and house yards of a Miao village form closed geometric shapes. These are polygons.
image_prompt: Show the overhead shapes of Miao village courtyards forming geometric patterns.

explanation_text: The folds of a Miao pleated skirt create triangle shapes as the cloth narrows toward the waist. Each fold is a triangle.
image_prompt: Show the triangular fold patterns formed by the pleats of a Miao skirt.

explanation_text: The square and rectangular motifs that fill a batik design form quadrilateral shapes with four sides each.
image_prompt: Show a batik cloth with repeating square and rectangular motifs.

explanation_text: Measuring the decorated border around a Miao pleated skirt is like finding the perimeter of a shape—the distance around its outside.
image_prompt: Show a pleated skirt with a dashed line tracing its decorated edge as the perimeter.

explanation_text: The amount of cloth covered by embroidery stitches on a Miao panel represents its area—the space inside a shape.
image_prompt: Show an embroidered cloth panel, shaded to show the area covered by stitches.

explanation_text: The amount of silver jewelry a storage box can hold represents its volume—the space inside a 3D shape.
image_prompt: Show wooden storage boxes filled with silver ornaments to different levels to illustrate volume.

miao_culture: Arc of the silver horn headdress
explanation_text: The curved arc of the silver horn headdress and the round silver neck rings are circles. They illustrate radius, diameter, and circumference.
image_prompt: Show a silver neck ring from above labeled with radius and diameter lines.

explanation_text: The relationship between the circumference and the diameter of a round silver neck ring is the constant ratio π, about 3.14.
image_prompt: Show a circular silver neck ring labeled with circumference and diameter measurements.

explanation_text: A batik design divided by horizontal and vertical wax lines resembles a coordinate grid, where each cell has its own position.
image_prompt: Show a batik grid map labeled with x and y coordinates.

miao_culture: Marking village houses on a map
explanation_text: Marking the location of each house in Xijiang village on a map is like plotting points on a coordinate plane.
image_prompt: Show a map of Xijiang village with labeled house locations marked as points.

explanation_text: The batik and embroidery designs on Miao clothing often mirror each other across a center line, showing symmetry.
image_prompt: Show a symmetrical batik and embroidery pattern split by a mirror line.

explanation_text: When lusheng dancers turn and shift positions during the Sister's Festival, they move shapes in space. These motions are geometric transformations.
image_prompt: Show lusheng dancers turning and shifting positions to illustrate transformations.

explanation_text: A festival outfit balances the amount of silver jewelry against the amount of cloth. This balance of two quantities is a ratio.
image_prompt: Show a Miao festival outfit labeled with silver-to-cloth ratio, like 2:1.

explanation_text: When a batik motif is scaled up for a larger cloth while every detail stays the same shape, the design keeps its proportion.
image_prompt: Show a small and large batik motif with the same geometric proportions.

explanation_text: The number of baskets of rice a family harvests in one day is a unit rate—a comparison for a single unit.
image_prompt: Show a rice harvest with the yield measured as baskets per day.

explanation_text: Drawing a smaller map of the large thousand-household village while keeping all distances proportional is a scale drawing.
image_prompt: Show Xijiang village and a smaller scaled map side by side with a scale legend.

explanation_text: If a family's silver ornaments grow from 100 pieces to 120 pieces, that is a 20% increase—an example of percent change.
image_prompt: Show a silver collection growing in number with a +20% label.

explanation_text: Recording how many households, cattle, and rice fields each part of the village has is an example of data collection.
image_prompt: Show a villager marking tallies of households and cattle on a clipboard.

explanation_text: Using a graph to show how many visitors came to the Sister's Festival each year helps visualize data trends.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph comparing festival visitors across several years.

explanation_text: Finding the average baskets of rice a field produces per season shows the mean.
image_prompt: Show a table of rice yields with an average value highlighted.

explanation_text: When family incomes are arranged from smallest to largest, the middle one is the median.
image_prompt: Show family incomes lined up with the middle one highlighted as the median.

explanation_text: If most headdresses in an area share the same silver pattern, that pattern is the mode—the most frequent value.
image_prompt: Show headdresses with various patterns, with one pattern being the most common.

explanation_text: The gap between the largest and smallest rice field shows the range of the data.
image_prompt: Show a chart with the shortest and tallest bars marked for range.

explanation_text: Each bar shows how many animals each family owns, making quick comparisons easy.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph labeled by family names with livestock totals.

explanation_text: A line graph shows how the rice harvest changes across the seasons of the year.
image_prompt: Show a line graph labeled with seasons and rice harvest amounts.

explanation_text: A pie chart can show the proportion of rice fields, forest, and housing in a Miao village.
image_prompt: Show a pie chart divided into land-use categories with percentages.

explanation_text: Estimating how likely rain is on Sister's Festival day involves probability—the chance of an event happening.
image_prompt: Show a festival scene with a weather prediction labeled with a probability percentage.

explanation_text: The motifs that repeat on silver bracelets and embroidered borders represent visual patterns, just as numbers repeat in sequences.
image_prompt: Show repeating geometric designs on Miao silver bracelets and embroidery.

explanation_text: If each worker carries a set number of rice baskets, every input gives one output. This one-to-one rule is a function.
image_prompt: Show a diagram linking each worker (input) to the rice baskets they carry (output).
